BACKGROUND

[7] The Appellant is a XXXX and retired XXXX XXXX. He started with the Nigerian police force (NPF) in XXXX XXXX and retired in 2009, with XXXX years of service. Throughout most of his career, he worked in the XXXX XXXX Division at various levels, moving up the ranks over the course of the years. In 2005, he became a XXXX. His father died in 1973, and his death was attributed to his refusal to become chief priest. After the Appellant's father's death, the Appellant was pressured to become chief priest, however, due to his role as a XXXX XXXX the agents of persecution could not exert influence over him.

[8] On XXXX XXXX, 2018, the Appellant was summoned to take over the role of chief priest. The Appellant also refused the position, however, in his case it was based on account of his Christian faith, and he was threatened with death for refusing. The Appellant relocated to XXXX; however, he received anonymous calls indicating that his whereabouts were known. On XXXX XXXX, 2019, the Appellant left Nigeria and travelled to the United States of America (USA). He did not claim asylum there due to anti-immigrant rhetoric, and then he travelled to Canada on October 4, 2019, and claimed asylum.

[14] The Appellant argues that the RPD breached natural justice because it allowed the Minister to file its notice of intervention which was, according to him, overly broad. The Appellant submits that in his case, the RPD failed to apply the guidelines as stated in the case of Baker.2 He submits that his refugee claim is a very important part of his life as it will have a great impact on his life if procedural fairness is not followed. He submits that the Minister initially indicated it would be intervening due to Article 1F(a) of the Convention and was then amended to include 1F(c) of the Convention. At the hearing, the Minister raised it would be intervening on Article 1F(b) of the Convention. The Appellant submits he was not given advance notice that Article 1F(b) of the Convention would be addressed, and he suggests the Minister was seeking any means to exclude him. He further submits that the Minister's notice of intervention also cited numerous sections of the Criminal Code of Canada (CCC) that it did not refer to in the hearing. The Appellant claims he was not aware of which issues he should have been prepared to respond to.

[15] I respectfully disagree with the Appellant. When turning to the RPD audio and transcript of the hearing,3 and all the evidence4 before the RPD, I find the RPD, and the Minister demonstrated procedural fairness. More specifically, the RPD and the Minister did not breach natural justice regarding the notice of exclusion under Article 1F(b). While the Minister's written notice of intervention and amended notice of intervention only stated it was intervening on exclusions of Articles 1F(a) and 1F(c), at the outset of the first RPD hearing in December 2021, the Minister corrected itself and said it was intervening on Article 1F(b).5 Upon the Minister doing so, the RPD immediately asked the Appellant's counsel whether he had any comments, to which he said he did not.6 The RPD hearing proceeded as scheduled, but the parties required more time for complete questioning. A second sitting was scheduled in February 2022 and the RPD also allowed both parties to file additional documentary evidence. The Appellant testified at both RPD sittings, December 9, 2021, and February 24, 2022, on issues regarding exclusion pursuant to Article 1F(b). The Minister provided oral submissions at the end of the February 2022 hearing regarding its position that the Appellant was excluded pursuant to Article 1F(b) of the Convention and under what sections of the CCC it was equivalencing his criminal acts committed, namely Section 120, Bribery of Officers and Section 346, Extortion.7

Complicity test set out in Ezokola

[42] As noted previously, the Appellant has acknowledged that if complicity is assumed, then the factors in Ezokola21 apply instead of guilt by association. While Ezokola addressed complicity in the context of an Article 1F(a) exclusion, it also commented on the applicability of subsection 21(2) of the CCC. As such, it adopted a contribution-based approach by establishing the requisite link between the individual and the group's criminal conduct. The accused's contribution does not have to be "directed to specific identifiable crimes" but can be directed to "wider concepts of common design, such as the accomplishment of an organisation's purpose by whatever means are necessary (...)".22

[43] Section 98 of the IRPA sets out that a person referred to in section F of Article 1 of the Refugee Convention is neither a Convention refugee nor person in need of protection. Article 1F(a), which is the relevant provision in this case, states that: The provisions of this Convention shall not apply to any person with respect to whom there are serious reasons for considering that: (a) he has committed a crime against peace, a war crime or a crime against humanity, as defined in the international instruments drawn up to make provision in respect of such crime. The SCC in Ezokola has confirmed that the standard of serious reasons to consider is lower than that of a balance of probabilities but higher than mere suspicion.23 Also notably in Ezokola, an individual need not have physically committed the crime but can be excluded where they are complicit in the crime.

[66] The crime of Bribery of Officers and Extorsion if committed in Canada are both indictable offenses and both are seen as serious under the CCC. Bribery holds a sentence of imprisonment for a term not exceeding 14 years. Extorsion, in his case scenario holds a sentence of life imprisonment.

[67] With regards to the elements of the crime related to the Bribery of Officers and Extortion, the RPD noted that the police and XXXX XXXX exercise power and authority over individuals, and the act of extortion involves exercising that power, likely through threats and coercion. It found his crimes were serious and pointed to documentary evidence that connects acts of extortion and bribery to other unlawful activities such as unlawful detention, physical violence, sexual assault, or murder.66 It found that the elements of the crime related to Bribery of Officers and Extortion, that police and XXXX XXXX exercise power and authority over individuals, and that the act of extortion involves exercising that power, likely through threats or coercion. It also found that both were indictable offenses and that the penalty for similar crimes in Canada is from 14 years to life imprisonment and his elevated position would result in a lengthier sentence, indicating that legislators consider the offence committed by the Appellant to be serious. In regard to the prescribed penalty, the Minister refers to sections 120 and 346(1) of the CCC, which indicate that the crimes are punishable in Canada by up to 14 years imprisonment or life imprisonment, respectively. The RPD found that, in light of the position of authority held by the Appellant when he carried out his crimes, the penalty applied would not be on the low end of the scale. As a result, it found that this factor supports the conclusion that the Appellant committed serious crimes.

Having considered the evidence of the Appellant's position of authority held in the XXXX XXXX Division of the NPF, I agree with the RPD that if committed in Canada that sentencing would range from 14 years to life and the penalty applied would not be on the low end of the scale given his authority within the police. This factor supports that the Appellant committed serious crimes. The RPD correctly concluded the same.

[57] The CCC paragraph 21(1)(b) or the doctrine of common intention under subsection 21(2) of the Criminal Code are as follows:
Parties to offence
21 (1) Every one is a party to an offence who
o (a) actually commits it;
o (b) does or omits to do anything for the purpose of aiding any person to commit it; or
o (c) abets any person in committing it.
Marginal note: Common intention
(2) Where two or more persons form an intention in common to carry out an unlawful purpose and to assist each other therein and any one of them, in carrying out the common purpose, commits an offence, each of them who knew or ought to have known that the commission of the offence would be a probable consequence of carrying out the common purpose is a party to that offence.

[58] In this case, the objective evidence points to the XXXX XXXX Division, committing bribery and extortion and as such. By being a XXXX XXXX, XXXX, XXXX and rising to the rank of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in the NPF, specifically in the XXXX XXXX Division as the Appellant was for years of his careers, and he omitted to do anything for the purpose of adding any person to commit it. The Appellant's oral testimony answers were general responses, using the pronouns "you" and "they" throughout his testimony to describe roles and activities and his responses tried to divert what he actually did, describing what "the XXXX XXXX personnel" did generally. The Appellant has attempted to convince the RPD and the RAD what "generally" happens instead of testifying to what he directly did, saw, or ignored. I find the Appellant's testimony evasive. This negatively impacts his credibility. I agree with the Minister that the doctrine of common intention applies in this case.

The crime of Bribery of Officers under section 120 of the CCC and the crime of Extortion under section 346 of the CCC are sufficient to find that the crime is serious to conclude that the Appellant is excluded. In coming to this finding, I have considered all the evidence.

Based on the evidence, there are serious reasons to consider that he has committed a non-political crime. The RPD was correct in coming to their conclusion but ought to have considered the complicity factors as per Ezokola.

REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW

[1] I dismiss this appeal brought by XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant). The Appellant appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated April 11, 2022, excluding him from refugee protection. The Appellant is excluded from refugee protection, pursuant to Article 1F(b) of the Convention. I confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is not a Convention refugee.

[2] The Appellant is a citizen of Nigeria. He made a refugee claim on the basis of religion. The Appellant alleges that he and his family are under threat because he was summoned to take over as chief priest, which he refused to do because it goes against his beliefs as a Christian and as a XXXX. He alleges that he can be killed by idol worshippers because of his refusal to take on the hereditary role. The Minister of Public Safety (the Minister) intervened at the RPD seeking an exclusion of the Appellant pursuant to Article 1F(b) of the United Nations Convention on the Status of Refugees (Convention) and section 98 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) - because he committed a serious non-political crime outside of Canada when he worked as a XXXX XXXX which would be equivalent to Bribery of Officers and Extortion in Canada under the doctrine of common intention. The RPD found the Minister had met his burden and excluded the Appellant.

[3] The Minister has not intervened at the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD). The determinative issue in this appeal is whether the RPD erred in its decision to exclude the Appellant. There is no new evidence in this appeal or request for an oral hearing. The Appellant argues that he is not excluded from refugee protection. He also argues there was a breach of natural justice made by the RPD.

[4] After reviewing the record, I determine that the RPD did not breach natural justice and that the test for exclusion is met, having considered the complicity test factors. The Appellant is excluded from refugee protection.
DECISION

[5] I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
ROLE OF THE RAD
[6] My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.1
BACKGROUND

[7] The Appellant is a XXXX and retired XXXX XXXX. He started with the Nigerian police force (NPF) in XXXX XXXX and retired in 2009, with XXXX years of service. Throughout most of his career, he worked in the XXXX XXXX Division at various levels, moving up the ranks over the course of the years. In 2005, he became a XXXX. The Appellant's family maintains a shrine which requires a priest. The Appellant's father refused to become chief priest of the shrine and fled from the village of XXXX XXXX. His father died in 1973, and his death was attributed to his refusal to become chief priest. After the Appellant's father's death, the Appellant was pressured to become chief priest, however, due to his role as a XXXX XXXX the agents of persecution could not exert influence over him.

[8] On XXXX XXXX, 2018, the Appellant was summoned to take over the role of chief priest. The Appellant also refused the position, however, in his case it was based on account of his Christian faith, and he was threatened with death for refusing. He alleges that three men followed him home that day and that he stayed indoors before he could report it to the police. Subsequently, the threats were reported to the police; however, the police took no action because it was a "family matter" and due to staff shortage of police officers. The Appellant relocated to XXXX; however, he received anonymous calls indicating that his whereabouts were known. On XXXX XXXX, 2019, the Appellant left Nigeria and travelled to the United States of America (USA). He did not claim asylum there due to anti-immigrant rhetoric, and then he travelled to Canada on October 4, 2019, and claimed asylum.

[9] The Minister initially intervened at the RPD in June 2021 and amended its notice of intervention in December 2021, on credibility and exclusion pursuant to Articles 1F(a) and (c). During the Appellant's RPD hearing, the Minister orally added exclusion pursuant to Article 1F(b). The Appellant's RPD hearing proceeded on the exclusion pursuant to Article 1F(b).
GROUNDS OF APPEAL
[10] The Appellant argues that the RPD breached procedural fairness and erred in finding him to be excluded pursuant to Article 1F(b) of the Convention.
ANALYSIS

[11] For this appeal, the central questions are: was there a denial of natural justice against the Appellant and is there serious reasons for considering that the Appellant committed a non-serious political crime thereby excluding him pursuant to Article 1F(b) from refugee protection? In order to address this question, I will address the issues that arise:
* Did the RPD breach natural justice by not allowing the Appellant the ability to respond to the exclusion pursuant to Article 1F(b)?
* Did the RPD err in finding a crime has been committed?
* Does the complicity framework of Ezokola apply to the commission of a non-serious political crime through the doctrine of common intention under Article 1F(b)?
* Did the Appellant commit Bribery of Officers and Extortion under the doctrine of common intention rendering him excluded pursuant to Article 1F(b) and section 98 of IRPA?

[12] I will address these issues throughout my decision.
The RPD did not breach natural justice

[13] The RPD did not breach natural justice. The Appellant was afforded the opportunity to know the case that needed to be met in order to respond to the intervention of the Minister regarding the exclusion pursuant to Article 1F(b).

[14] The Appellant argues that the RPD breached natural justice because it allowed the Minister to file its notice of intervention which was, according to him, overly broad. The Appellant submits that in his case, the RPD failed to apply the guidelines as stated in the case of Baker.2 He submits that his refugee claim is a very important part of his life as it will have a great impact on his life if procedural fairness is not followed. He submits that the Minister initially indicated it would be intervening due to Article 1F(a) of the Convention and was then amended to include 1F(c) of the Convention. At the hearing, the Minister raised it would be intervening on Article 1F(b) of the Convention. The Appellant submits he was not given advance notice that Article 1F(b) of the Convention would be addressed, and he suggests the Minister was seeking any means to exclude him. He further submits that the Minister's notice of intervention also cited numerous sections of the Criminal Code of Canada (CCC) that it did not refer to in the hearing. The Appellant claims he was not aware of which issues he should have been prepared to respond to.

[15] I respectfully disagree with the Appellant. When turning to the RPD audio and transcript of the hearing,3 and all the evidence4 before the RPD, I find the RPD, and the Minister demonstrated procedural fairness. More specifically, the RPD and the Minister did not breach natural justice regarding the notice of exclusion under Article 1F(b). While the Minister's written notice of intervention and amended notice of intervention only stated it was intervening on exclusions of Articles 1F(a) and 1F(c), at the outset of the first RPD hearing in December 2021, the Minister corrected itself and said it was intervening on Article 1F(b).5 Upon the Minister doing so, the RPD immediately asked the Appellant's counsel whether he had any comments, to which he said he did not.6 The RPD hearing proceeded as scheduled, but the parties required more time for complete questioning. A second sitting was scheduled in February 2022 and the RPD also allowed both parties to file additional documentary evidence. The Appellant testified at both RPD sittings, December 9, 2021, and February 24, 2022, on issues regarding exclusion pursuant to Article 1F(b). The Minister provided oral submissions at the end of the February 2022 hearing regarding its position that the Appellant was excluded pursuant to Article 1F(b) of the Convention and under what sections of the CCC it was equivalencing his criminal acts committed, namely Section 120, Bribery of Officers and Section 346, Extortion.7

[16] In addition to that the Minister filed oral submissions (notes) and then amended written submissions (notes) of its oral submissions on the record.8 The Appellant was given the opportunity to provide written submissions on the Article 1F(b) exclusion.9 The Appellant took advantage of the opportunity to file written submissions on March 27, 2022, on the issue of Article 1F(b) exclusion.10 Given the Minister had the burden to prove its arguments, the Minister filed reply submissions.11

[17] Based on all the evidence before me, the Appellant was given notice at the outset of the December 2021 hearing that the Minister would be asking the RPD to exclude him pursuant to Article 1F(b). It was open to the Appellant and his Counsel to request an adjournment when the Minister clarified the grounds upon which he was seeking exclusion. The Appellant did not make this request. The RPD accepted the Minister's change as the Appellant made no objection to it and the refugee claim proceeded on exclusion. The Appellant was subsequently asked questions exclusively on exclusion matters and he provided answers to those questions. More importantly, he provided written submissions on Article 1F(b), having been granted the opportunity to do so in writing rather than orally. The RPD considered the Appellant's submissions12 in its reasons to exclude him. The Appellant did not lack the opportunity to know the case to meet or to respond to the arguments of the Minister. The RPD nor the Minister did not breach natural justice as alleged by the Appellant. Based on all the evidence, there is no evidence to support the Appellant's argument regarding a breach of natural justice by the RPD.
EXCLUSION
THE RPD CORRECTLY FOUND THE APPELLANT WAS EXCLUDED PURSUANT TO ARTICLE 1F(B)

[18] The RPD correctly assessed that the commission of a crime has been proven and excluded the Appellant pursuant to Article 1F(b).
RPD finding on exclusion

[19] The RPD agreed with the Minister's submissions. Its reasons for coming to this conclusion will be addressed throughout my reasons.
Appellant's arguments on appeal

[20] The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in finding he is excluded from Article 1F(b) of the Convention. His submissions on where the RPD erred will be considered throughout my reasons.
The Minister's intervention and evidence at the RPD

[21] The Minister intervened in person before the RPD alleging the Appellant was excluded from refugee protection as there are serious reasons for considering that he had committed a serious non-political offence prior to his entry into Canada. The Minister submitted the following before the RPD:
* In Nigeria, the national police force and the XXXX XXXX are highly corrupted, and that members of these forces are expected to contribute to a system of returns.
* The Appellant was a member of the NPF XXXX XXXX department, also known as the XXXX XXXX in Lagos, Nigeria, where he rose the ranks from XXXX to become a XXXX XXXX XXXX, as XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.
* That the Appellant participated in the widespread use of extortion to obtain bribes and contributed to this system by moving money up the chain of command.
* That there are serious reasons for considering the Appellant was complicit in the commission of crime in Nigeria by operation of paragraph 21(1)(b) or the doctrine of common intention under subsection 21(2) of the CCC. Those crimes in Canada would be:
o Bribery of Officers (s. 120 CCC), the penalty for which can be imprisonment for a term not exceeding fourteen years.
o Extortion (s. 346 CCC), the penalty for which can be imprisonment for life.
RAD assessment of exclusion

[22] In assessing whether the RPD was incorrect in their finding and assessment of the evidence regarding the Appellant's exclusion based on the arguments submitted by the Appellant, I will assess the arguments on appeal based on the below findings.
Applicable legal principles

[23] The Minister bears the onus of proving that a claimant is excluded from refugee protection pursuant to Article 1F(b) of the Convention. That is, the Minister bears the onus of establishing that there are "serious reasons for considering" that a claimant has committed a serious non-political crime.13

[24] A crime will generally be considered as serious where a maximum sentence of 10 years or more could have been imposed had the crime been committed in Canada. However, this is a rebuttable presumption. In Jayasekara, the Federal Court of Appeal found that, when assessing the seriousness of a crime, it is necessary to consider the elements of the crime, the mode of prosecution, the penalty prescribed, the facts, and the mitigating and aggravating circumstances underlying the conviction.14 In Febles, the Supreme Court of Canada cautioned that decision-makers must not apply the ten-year sentence rule in an unjust, mechanistic or decontextualized manner.15

[25] The RPD correctly applied the jurisprudence on Article 1F(b). The RPD found that the Minister had established that there was a serious reason for considering that the Appellant committed a serious, non-political crime prior to his entry into Canada. In addition, the RPD explained in its reasons how the Minister had established that the Appellant should be excluded pursuant to Article 1F(b) of the Convention and section 98 of the IRPA.
The RPD correctly found that a crime has been proven

[26] The RPD correctly found that the Minister has proven a crime has been committed. In applying the complicity factors which I find to be applicable to Article 1F(b), the RPD end result on exclusion is the same. The Appellant committed a non-political crime of Bribery of Officers and Extortion in Nigeria.
The RPD finding that there was a serious reason for considering the Appellant has committed a serious non-political offence, namely Bribery of Officers and Extortion, in Nigeria

[27] The RPD found that the Minister's evidence16 includes articles and documents from Human Rights Watch, the U.S. Department of State, the United Nations, and Amnesty International. The Minister's representative also provided reports and articles that specifically focus on XXXX XXXX. The RPD found the Minister's evidence indicates:
* that police in Nigeria are corrupt and demand bribes and extort members of the public;
* that police officers must pay their superiors to be assigned to lucrative posts where they can elicit bribes;17
* that the Appellant worked in a sought-after post XXXX XXXX in Lagos, and was employed within the XXXX XXXX XXXX for XXXX years where he was promoted several times to become XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX; and
* that evidence indicates that XXXX XXXX within the Nigerian police XXXX XXXX XXXX that cause XXXX in order to elicit bribes from XXXX.

[28] The RPD did not accept the Appellant's explanation that he was unaware of corruption (bribes and extortion), given evidence that corruption among XXXX XXXX is endemic and hierarchical. It also highlighted that his lengthy career with the police and his promotions were indicative of his participation in Bribery of Officers. It also found that the Appellant aided his colleagues in accepting bribes, and that the offence if committed in Canada would be Bribery of Officers and Extortion.

[29] The Appellant argues the RPD erred in finding there was serious reason for finding that he has committed a serious non-political offence. He submits the RPD failed to consider that he did not commit any crimes and was not convicted. The Appellant argues with the RPD's finding that he was complicit due to his employment with the Nigerian police. He submits that complicity is addressed pursuant to Article 1F(a) and not Article1F(b), and the Appellant would not be excluded even pursuant to Article 1F(a). He submits that the RPD's reference to a "common intent doctrine" is not associated with Article 1F(b) assessments. The Appellant also argues the RPD erred in finding there was serious reason for finding the Appellant has committed a serious non-political offence prior to entering Canada, namely Bribery of Officers and Extortion.

[30] He submits that promotions in the Nigerian police were assigned based on geographical quotas; impoverished individuals from Northern Nigeria were more often selected for promotions and that the Appellant indicated he was underpaid but was content with his salary. He also submits the RPD failed to consider that he retired from the police force in 2009, that the evidence submitted by the Minister post-dates the Appellant's retirement, and that the Minister did not address his specific unit within the police where he worked.

[31] The RPD correctly concluded there was a serious reason for concluding that the Appellant aided his colleagues in accepting bribes, and that the offence if committed in Canada would be Bribery of Officers and Extortion. When I apply the complicity framework and the doctrine of common intent, these reasons further support the RPD conclusion.
The Appellant's involvement in the crime

[32] The Appellant's involvement in the crime is essential in concluding his exclusion pursuant to Article 1F (b). In order to do so, I have applied the complicity framework to assess his involvement in the crime alleged by the Minister, namely Bribery by Officer and Extortion.
The Appellant's actions should be analysed under the complicity framework

[33] The Minister has not produced any evidence that the Appellant was personally involved and the Appellant himself has denied any knowledge or involvement. As previously indicated, the Minister has submitted that para. 21(1)(b) or the doctrine of common intention under subsection 21(2) of the CCC apply to exclude the Appellant pursuant to Article 1F(b). The Minister argues the Appellant was complicit by virtue of the aforementioned CCC provisions while the Appellant argues that the concept of complicity does not apply pursuant to 1(F)(b).

[34] For clarity purposes, in this case, there is no evidence that the Appellant was directly involved in accepting bribes but that the Minister argued he was complicit under the doctrine of common intention as noted above. The RPD did not assess the exclusion under the complicity framework. The RAD will assess whether the Appellant meets the test for complicity.

[35] The onus to establish serious reasons that need to be taken into consideration is on the Minister to address. Meeting this onus requires precision in identifying exactly what alleged crimes the Appellant had committed and showing what evidence meets the requisite threshold. I find the Minister has met the onus to establish serious reasons for considering the Appellant has committed a serious non-political crime. Therefore, I will examine the Appellant's actions under the framework of complicity set out by the Supreme Court of Canada (SCC).
Complicity

[36] As explained in Zrig v. Canada, ("Zrig") 2003 FCA 178, there is no requirement that a person being charged or convicted for the exclusion to apply. As such, the Appellant's argument on the point that he was not charged or convicted must fail.

[37] The Appellant's argument is that complicity is addressed pursuant to Article 1F(a) and not 1F(b). Through this argument, the Appellant seems to suggest that complicity does not apply for a Article1F(b) exclusion. However, he concedes that if complicity is assumed, the factors set out by the SCC in Ezokola18 must be used rather than the issue being decided on the basis of guilt by association.

[38] Interestingly, the Appellant argues19 that in Zrig, the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) has opined that complicity applies to Article 1F(a) but not 1(F)(b). This is incorrect. The Appellant is citing a dissenting judge. Contrary to this assertion, the FCA Zrig decision stands for the proposition that the concept of complicity applicable to Article 1F(a) also applies to 1F(b) (see paras 92 to 98). Moreover, the Appellant argues that Febles20 stands for the proposition that Article 1F(b) does not extend to include members of an organization that had contributed to the organization's crime. In fact, the SCC only addresses Article 1F(b) in relation to the individual at issue (i.e., Mr. Febles).

[39] Admittedly, issues related to the commission of crime by a state or state actors in past cases include crimes pursuant to Article 1F(a) and where the issue of complicity is almost always in play. Moreover, pursuant to Article 1F(a), the crimes involved are the most serious as recognized by the international community such as but not limited to war crimes. It is understandable that crimes that do not rise to this level involving states or state actors would not occur frequently. Nevertheless, as exemplified by this case, they may occur.

[40] The principles of complicity applicable to Article 1F(a) may be applicable to Article 1F(b) and (c) as well. In addition to being consistent with the approach to 1F(a) internationally, the Court found that it was also consistent with "s. 21(2) of the Canadian Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, which attaches criminal liability based on assistance in carrying out a common unlawful purpose". Given the Minister is relying on 21(2) of the CCC to bring the Appellant within the Article 1F(b) exclusion, my analysis includes the contribution made by the Appellant to the common unlawful purpose that is alleged in this case, that is Bribery of Officer and extortion.

[41] The documentation appears to show a widespread system of bribes to officers and extortions by a state organization and its employees and the Appellant's participation by virtue of the application of subsection 20(2) of the CCC. In my view, the test for complicity as set out in Ezokola provides a good road map to assess these arguments.
Complicity test set out in Ezokola

[42] As noted previously, the Appellant has acknowledged that if complicity is assumed, then the factors in Ezokola21 apply instead of guilt by association. While Ezokola addressed complicity in the context of an Article 1F(a) exclusion, it also commented on the applicability of subsection 21(2) of the CCC. As such, it adopted a contribution-based approach by establishing the requisite link between the individual and the group's criminal conduct. The accused's contribution does not have to be "directed to specific identifiable crimes" but can be directed to "wider concepts of common design, such as the accomplishment of an organisation's purpose by whatever means are necessary (...)".22

[43] Section 98 of the IRPA sets out that a person referred to in section F of Article 1 of the Refugee Convention is neither a Convention refugee nor person in need of protection. Article 1F(a), which is the relevant provision in this case, states that: The provisions of this Convention shall not apply to any person with respect to whom there are serious reasons for considering that: (a) he has committed a crime against peace, a war crime or a crime against humanity, as defined in the international instruments drawn up to make provision in respect of such crime. The SCC in Ezokola has confirmed that the standard of serious reasons to consider is lower than that of a balance of probabilities but higher than mere suspicion.23 Also notably in Ezokola, an individual need not have physically committed the crime but can be excluded where they are complicit in the crime.

[45] The SCC has held that a significant contribution need not mean a contribution which is directed to specific and identifiable crimes but could be actions directed to the common design of the organization. I will assess the Appellant's degree of contribution bearing in mind the Court's caution that almost any act in furtherance of a group could further its criminal purpose, and the contribution must be carefully assessed to determine if it is significant.26 For the following reasons, the Appellant's actions constitute a significant contribution.
Evidence of significant contribution

[46] The size and nature of organization: the NPF is nationally spread over 36 states with upwards of 375,000 members strong. The Appellant admits the XXXX XXXXDivision falls under the NPF. The NPF can also be described as committing systemic, institutionalized, and widespread serious non-political crimes with almost total impunity27 when considering bribery and extortion made by police personnel.

[47] The part of the organization with which the Appellant was most directly concerned: The parties agree that the Appellant worked for the NPF, he was a XXXX XXXX at the beginning of his career and worked his way up the NPF in the XXXX XXXXDivision as an XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. He also had men under his command. His role in the NPF is significant.

[48] The Appellant worked for XXXX years as a XXXX XXXX with the Nigerian Police. For the majority of his career he worked for the XXXX XXXX XXXX, at various levels including a XXXX who reports to a XXXX.28 His tasks included the XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX.29 He did not XXXX XXXX XXXX as XXXX XXXX are stationed for XXXX XXXX as well.30 He said as a XXXX between XXXX and XXXX, he did not make arrests but it is under his discretion.31 He confirmed on one occasion he arrested a person and took them to the station and wrote a statement in case he needed to give evidence which is taken to the Magistrate Courts or XXXX XXXX.32 He said people would not be detained for XXXX more than 24 hours. He specified that usually officers write their reports with the exception of XXXX XXXX XXXX, the person could be held longer through a Court order.33

[49] His duties and activities: First, the Appellant worked in the XXXX XXXX Division of the Police since the early XXXX. The evidence supports that XXXX XXXX officers under the Nigerian National Police ask for bribes from XXXX and extort them for financial gain. The evidence shows that police and XXXX XXXX demand bribes from the public. Notably, the 2008 report of the second Presidential Committee on Police Reform acknowledged that police are perceived as one of the most corrupt government institutions in Nigeria, with personnel constantly accused of bribery and extortion in the course of performing their functions.34 The period covered by this report does address the period that the Appellant was a XXXX XXXX. During XXXX XXXX XXXX, he worked night, day, and afternoon shifts.35 He testified to hearing things were happening but not seeing them.36 The later years of his career he was a XXXX, XXXX rising to the rank of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX for the NPF.37 I disagree with the Appellant's arguments that the evidence in the record post-dates his work with the police and that his unit is not named, the forementioned evidence contradicts his assertion.

[50] In summary, over his career of XXXX years, the Appellant instructed other XXXX XXXX in the XXXX XXXX Division at all levels,38 conducted XXXX XXXX to control them,39 and had people under him and supervised other XXXX XXXX XXXX.40

[51] The recent Federal Court (FC) decision in Kurt,41 found that supervisory responsibility is not a requirement for complicity under the contribution-based test outlined by the SCC. For the purposes of this appeal, I am also not weighing this factor pursuant to Article 1F(b) complicity exclusion. I am weighing the complicity factors to determine if the Appellant is excluded pursuant to Article 1F(b) for having committed a serious non-political crime. The FC in Kurt, though in the context of an Article 1F(a) exclusion also found that culpable conduct can take many forms. Supervisory responsibility is not a requirement for complicity under the contribution-based test.42 In this case, I am introducing the Appellant's XXXX role as a fact and link it to his overall conduct and knowledge as a XXXX XXXX XXXX under the NPF and whether he is complicit in committing a serious non-political crime.43 I consider his XXXX role as part of the doctrine of common intention and exclusion pursuant to Article 1F(b).

[52] The Appellant's position and rank in the organization: Second, his activities and rank changed over the years, from XXXX, to XXXX to XXXX, and lastly to XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. He became XXXX in the Police, by way of promotion44 and denied bribing instructors for his promotion, saying his was meritorious.45 As a XXXX XXXX, he had more responsibilities. He was taking commands from his senior, and he had people to command and instruct working under him.46 He said they have XXXX courses but did not answer the question whether he had to take courses to be promoted to XXXX, noting he was very intelligent and taught courses being a XXXX.47 After two to three years of being XXXX, he became a XXXX "just like that", an automatic promotion no course required.48 He was a XXXX from 1994 to 1998, but started more responsibilities as a XXXX before it happened.49 He denied knowing that colleagues and other trainers, at the academy received bribes from trainees who wanted to learn and then said some may have, some officers do such a thing that impacted "us" the policemen were dismissed.50

[53] He declared that the police in Nigeria were underpaid but he was content, he lived within the limits of his income.51 He testified52 that he did not know if it was common for civilians to give money to the police, and he has never taken any money. He added he was a disciplined man, brought up Christian who fears God. He denies accepting any money or bribes and to his knowledge he said he is not aware of police officers taking bribes.53 At the second hearing he said there was no way they did not have "bad eggs" because everyone has them, but that his background as a Christian, he's a XXXX, he does not indulge in it and he condemns it, he XXXX against it.54 He added that if any malfeasance happened it was because of a lack of supervision and the officer in charge should be held responsible first, noting it is the delegation of duty and he won't allow it.55 When answering a question by the Minister regarding what the role of the XXXX department was when it comes to organizing or manning a XXXX on the XXXX, he said there could sometimes be XXXX XXXX but he does not participate because he did not want to be corrupted.56 He also said they did not do XXXX but XXXX XXXX.57 He said the XXXX XXXX division within the police were responsible for XXXX, XXXX duties, XXXX management, XXXX avoidance by encouraging XXXX to obey the XXXX XXXX, rules, regulations, created awareness of XXXX XXXX, and XXXX according to the XXXX.58

[54] The Appellant rising to the rank of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in the NPF was significant for him to see and know what was going on which makes it more difficult for him to plead ignorance. Though he denies being involved in bribery and extortion, the objective evidence references that it is police personnel, often in groups, that extort money from XXXX and systematically bribe for money for right of passage59 makes it very difficult for me to credibly find his testimony that he has never bribed/extorted anyone or seen anyone involved in such a thing especially given he achieved a fairly senior rank of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. His statement that "could sometimes be XXXX XXXX but he does not participate because he did not want to be corrupted" contradicts his denial of knowing and is an admission that he knew there was corrupt behaviour. At the very least it points to him knowing it must have happened. I considered his testimony regarding his religious beliefs and that being a XXXX he cannot engage in malfeasance because he comes to XXXX and as a XXXX, he does not tell lies.60 Despite his religious beliefs, he has not convinced me that even as a XXXX who believes he cannot engage in malfeasance, would prevent him from doing nothing especially since he admits to knowing that this "could sometimes" happen. He still does not directly admit to knowing, seeing, or hearing about this regular systemic bribery and extortion by the XXXX XXXX personnel. He has, however, given nuanced evidence by stating there are "bad apples" which demonstrates to me that he had some knowledge that "something bad" was going on. His admission of knowing but did not participate because he did not want to be corrupt also contradicts his direct denial. Also, in other parts of his testimony, he did not deny the fact that he heard or had knowledge that bribery of officers and extortion was happening. In addition, the newspapers in Nigeria also would have informed him of the public perception of XXXX XXXX extorting money, which he said was not done in his presence.61 His religious beliefs and role as a XXXX do not exclude him from committing and knowing this was happening. Being religious also does not prevent him from knowing or seeing what is happening, namely that Bribery of Officers and Extortion was happening for the financial gain of the police personnel which was outside of their role of easing XXXX XXXX and educating the public on XXXX, etc.

[55] The length of time the Appellant was in the organization, particularly after acquiring knowledge of the group's crime or criminal purpose: It has been decades since the NPF has had criminal purpose and corrupt. The Appellant's XXXX years of service provided him with the lengthy experience, including achieving a senior rank, and the knowledge of its organization's criminal purpose and corruption. Moreover, the Nigerian reports of the 2008 Presidential Committee on Police Reform acknowledged that police are perceived as one of the most corrupt government institutions in Nigeria, with personnel constantly accused of bribery and extortion in the course of performing their functions.62 The Appellant was working during this timeframe when the briberies and extortion by XXXX XXXX purported the NPF's criminal purpose and corruption were happening which also weighs negatively in his case.

[56] Opportunity to leave the organization: The Appellant voluntarily remained in the NPF and retired from their organization. He chose not to leave the organization and achieved a fairly senior rank of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. This points to him being complicit and ignoring the bribery and extortion happening around him if not participate.
Paragraph 21(1)(b) or the doctrine of common intention under subsection 21(2) of the CCC apply to exclude the Appellant pursuant to Article 1F(b)

[57] The CCC paragraph 21(1)(b) or the doctrine of common intention under subsection 21(2) of the Criminal Code are as follows:
Parties to offence
21 (1) Every one is a party to an offence who
o (a) actually commits it;
o (b) does or omits to do anything for the purpose of aiding any person to commit it; or
o (c) abets any person in committing it.
Marginal note: Common intention
(2) Where two or more persons form an intention in common to carry out an unlawful purpose and to assist each other therein and any one of them, in carrying out the common purpose, commits an offence, each of them who knew or ought to have known that the commission of the offence would be a probable consequence of carrying out the common purpose is a party to that offence.

[58] In this case, the objective evidence points to the XXXX XXXX Division, committing bribery and extortion and as such. By being a XXXX XXXX, XXXX, XXXX and rising to the rank of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in the NPF, specifically in the XXXX XXXX Division as the Appellant was for years of his careers, and he omitted to do anything for the purpose of adding any person to commit it. The Appellant's oral testimony answers were general responses, using the pronouns "you" and "they" throughout his testimony to describe roles and activities and his responses tried to divert what he actually did, describing what "the XXXX XXXX personnel" did generally. The Appellant has attempted to convince the RPD and the RAD what "generally" happens instead of testifying to what he directly did, saw, or ignored. I find the Appellant's testimony evasive. This negatively impacts his credibility. I agree with the Minister that the doctrine of common intention applies in this case.

[59] Through the complicity assessment above, I find the Minister has made his case. The Appellant is complicit through the doctrine of common intention. The crime of Bribery of Officers under section 120 of the CCC and the crime of Extortion under section 346 of the CCC are sufficient to find that the crime is serious to conclude that the Appellant is excluded. In coming to this finding, I have considered all the evidence.

[60] I do not find the RPD made an incorrect finding on Article 1F(b) as the Appellant argues. The RPD correctly applied the evidence to the caselaw in assessing Article 1F(b) and as the Minister argued complicity at the RPD, I expanded that assessment to consider complicity factors in accordance with the SCC guidance in Ezokola and how they apply to the doctrine of common intention pursuant to Article 1F(b). The RAD has not raised a new issue within the exclusion analysis that required giving the Appellant notice. The Appellant has not rebutted the Minister's allegations as his testimony and evidence provided to do so have serious credibility and trustworthiness issues. Based on the evidence, there are serious reasons to consider that he has committed a non-political crime. The RPD was correct in coming to their conclusion but ought to have considered the complicity factors as per Ezokola.
The Appellant's testimony and evidence before the RPD is not credible

[61] The Appellant's testimony was vague at times. There were instances when he needed to be redirected to answer the question.63 He commonly differed to providing examples of what the common group did or did not do while he was working, and his denial of the commonly objective evidence that police and XXXX XXXX in Nigeria asked for bribes and extorted from their citizens is not believable. He regularly diverted the questions by comparing Nigerian "bad apples" to what could happen in various cities of Canada. Overall, the RPD was correct to find it was not credible that he was generally unaware of corruption and the system of passing proceeds from extortion and bribes up the ranks.

[62] The Appellant worked for the NPF XXXX XXXX Division, also known as the XXXX XXXX in Lagos, Nigeria, where he was promoted to higher rankings under the Nigerian National Police. Though the Appellant says he was only a XXXX XXXX and not a member of the regular police, this does not matter. The Appellant worked for the NPF in the XXXX XXXX Division. In light of the documentary evidence about the criminal behaviour of those XXXX XXXX engaged in XXXX enforcement, I see no distinction between being a XXXX XXXX or a regular police officer.

[63] I find the RPD did consider that the Appellant has been retired since 2009. The RPD reasons clearly state that the evidence shows that police and XXXX XXXX demand bribes from the public. Notably, the 2008 report of the second Presidential Committee on Police Reform acknowledged that police are perceived as one of the most corrupt government institutions in Nigeria, with personnel constantly accused of bribery and extortion in the course of performing their functions.64 This demonstrates to me that despite the Appellant being retired since 2009, the RPD found that while he was working as a XXXX XXXX, he need not demand for bribes or extort from the public during the course of his duties to have been complicit in the doctrine of common intention. The intention of the NPF was to carry out an unlawful purpose. The Appellant ought to have known that the commission of the offence would be a probable consequence of carrying out the common purpose and therefore the Appellant is a party to that offence.

[64] Overall, on the determinative issue, I find the Appellant's evidence not credible. Particularly that he alleges he did not have any knowledge or see any bribery by officers or extortion over the course of his career. His testimony that he did not agree or need it because he was a religious man and had the support of his wife bears no weight on the fact that the objective evidence points to the Nigerian police and XXXX XXXX committing bribery and extortion. He is not a credible witness, and his testimony did not rebut the Minister's allegations.
There are serious reasons to consider the Appellant committed a non-political crime therefore excluding him from refugee protection

[65] Based on the evidence provided, I find the crime of Bribery by officers and Extortion was committed for economic reasons; there was no political purpose to the crimes. The Minister has met their burden of demonstrating so, and the RPD did not err. The crime is non-political for the purposes of Article 1F(b) of the Convention.65 The Appellant is excluded from refugee protection.
The Crime Committed as Viewed by Canadian Law

[66] The crime of Bribery of Officers and Extorsion if committed in Canada are both indictable offenses and both are seen as serious under the CCC. Bribery holds a sentence of imprisonment for a term not exceeding 14 years. Extorsion, in his case scenario holds a sentence of life imprisonment.
Seriousness of the crimes

[67] With regards to the elements of the crime related to the Bribery of Officers and Extortion, the RPD noted that the police and XXXX XXXX exercise power and authority over individuals, and the act of extortion involves exercising that power, likely through threats and coercion. It found his crimes were serious and pointed to documentary evidence that connects acts of extortion and bribery to other unlawful activities such as unlawful detention, physical violence, sexual assault, or murder.66 It found that the elements of the crime related to Bribery of Officers and Extortion, that police and XXXX XXXX exercise power and authority over individuals, and that the act of extortion involves exercising that power, likely through threats or coercion. The RPD found that the documentary evidence connects acts of extortion and bribery to other unlawful activities, such as unlawful detention, physical and sexual assault, torture or even murder.67 Consequently, the RPD found that the constituent elements of such an offence supports the conclusion that the crimes are serious. It also found that both were indictable offenses and that the penalty for similar crimes in Canada is from 14 years to life imprisonment and his elevated position would result in a lengthier sentence, indicating that legislators consider the offence committed by the Appellant to be serious. In regard to the prescribed penalty, the Minister refers to sections 120 and 346(1) of the CCC, which indicate that the crimes are punishable in Canada by up to 14 years imprisonment or life imprisonment, respectively. The RPD found that, in light of the position of authority held by the Appellant when he carried out his crimes, the penalty applied would not be on the low end of the scale. As a result, it found that this factor supports the conclusion that the Appellant committed serious crimes.

[68] The Appellant has not made specific submissions on the RPD finding regarding the seriousness of the crimes. The evidence the RPD relied on further states:68 "Extortion-related confrontations between the police and XXXX often escalate into more serious abuses. The police have on numerous occasions severely beaten, sexually assaulted, or shot to death ordinary citizens who failed to pay bribes demanded." Later stating that "XXXX are frequently detained and endure harassment and threats until they or their family members negotiate payment for their release." Furthermore, the Human Rights Watch 2010, qualifies that the NPF, established in 1930, has a long history of engaging in unprofessional, corrupt, and criminal conduct, therefore I am convinced by the objective evidence that the Appellant's XXXX XXXXyear career was within the timeframe of this evidence in the record and contradicts his assertion that it was only after he left the NPF that this evidence occurred. Having considered the evidence of the Appellant's position of authority held in the XXXX XXXX Division of the NPF, I agree with the RPD that if committed in Canada that sentencing would range from 14 years to life and the penalty applied would not be on the low end of the scale given his authority within the police. This factor supports that the Appellant committed serious crimes. The RPD correctly concluded the same.
Mitigating factors not relevant to assessing the seriousness of a crime pursuant to Article 1F(b)

[69] The RPD did not need to assess mitigating factors according to the jurisprudence pursuant to Article 1F(b). The Appellant's arguments that the RPD erred in considering factors that would mitigate his exclusion does not matter.

[70] The RPD found that the pervasive nature of corruption and the Appellant's denial of participation in corruption were aggravating factors. It also found that his role as a XXXX was a mitigating factor, however it was not sufficient to outweigh the other considerations.

[71] The Appellant argues that the RPD erred by failing to consider factors which would mitigate the Appellant's exclusion that: he was forthcoming about his employment in the police; he was not a XXXX XXXX since 2009; his promotions were received over a long career, demonstrating that they were not achieved by corrupt means; he became a XXXX in 2005; he could rely on his family members for financial support and did not need to solicit bribes; and that there was no evidence that he accepted bribes.

[72] The SCC in Febles69 tells us that factors extraneous to the crime itself should not be considered. This approach has been followed in other decisions, such as Lin.70 The RPD must meaningfully grapple with whether the crime falls within the less serious, or the more serious range of the CCC provision. Similar to the jurisprudence aforementioned, I am not persuaded the RPD should be asked to do more. Mitigating factors was not a determinative issue before the RPD, and I am unable to see the need for it to have even assessed the noted mitigating factors. The RPD correctly found there were no mitigating factors even though it did not have to assess mitigating factors in the first place. Post-offence conduct is not relevant to assessing the seriousness of a crime pursuant to Article 1F(b). I reject the Appellant's argument that the RPD erred when it did not find mitigating factors in his case.
RAD finds that there are serious reasons to consider the Appellant committed a serious non-political crime and is therefore excluded from refugee protection

[73] For the above-mentioned reasons, there are serious reasons for considering that the Appellant committed a serious, non-political crime, that is extortion and bribery, prior to his entry into Canada by virtue of his participation in application of subsection 21(2) of the CCC and in keeping with the test for complicity set out in Ezokola.
[74] Accordingly, the Appellant is excluded from refugee protection in Canada by virtue of Article 1F(b) of the Convention and section 98 of the IRPA.
CONCLUSION

[75] I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
